claims.evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 caption with citation to Lang et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Nontransitive interactions among extant species are well documented as contributors to biological diversity and community structure.
claims.source: In ecology, nontransitive interactions among extant species are well documented as contributors to biological diversity and community structure (Kerr et al., 2002; Károlyi et al., 2005; Laird and Schamp, 2006; Reichenbach et al., 2007; Menezes et al., 2019) and arise by way of resource (Sinervo and Lively, 1996; Precoda et al., 2017) or interference competition (Kirkup and Riley, 2004).
claims.evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to ecological studies.

claims.claim: The importance of nontransitivity in ecology was first put forward in the 1970s.
claims.source: First put forward in the 1970s (Gilpin, 1975; Jackson and Buss, 1975; May and Leonard, 1975; Petraitis, 1979), the importance of nontransitivity in ecology has garnered extensive theoretical and experimental consideration over the last half century (e.g. Sinervo and Lively, 1996; Kerr et al., 2002; Allesina and Levine, 2011; Rojas-Echenique and Allesina, 2011; Soliveres et al., 2015; Liao et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to papers from the 1970s.

claims.claim: Testing for nontransitive interactions along lines of genealogical descent is not possible in natural populations because it requires the ability to directly compete an organism against its extinct genealogical ancestors.
claims.source: Testing the hypothesis that nontransitive interactions arise along lines of genealogical descent, however, is not possible in natural populations because it requires our ability to directly compete an organism against its immediate predecessor as well as against its extinct genealogical ancestors.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a logical constraint on studying natural populations.

claims.claim: Laboratory experimental evolution, in which populations are preserved as a 'frozen fossil record', affords the unique opportunity to test for nontransitivity along a genealogical lineage.
claims.source: Fortunately, laboratory experimental evolution, in which populations are preserved as a 'frozen fossil record', affords us with the unique opportunity to test for nontransitivity along a genealogical lineage by directly competing a given genotype against the extant as well as the extinct.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a rationale for using experimental evolution.

claims.claim: An early study of laboratory evolution of yeast in glucose-limited chemostats appeared to demonstrate that nontransitive interactions arise along a line of genealogical descent.
claims.source: An early study of laboratory evolution of yeast in glucose-limited chemostats appeared to demonstrate that nontransitive interactions arise along a line of genealogical descent (Paquin and Adams, 1983).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citation to Paquin and Adams, 1983.

claims.claim: The specific events that led to nontransitivity in the Paquin and Adams study are unknown.
claims.source: However, the specific events that led to nontransitivity in this case are unknown, and it is likely the case that the authors were measuring interactions between contemporaneous lineages in a population, rather than individuals along a direct line of genealogical descent, as they report (see Discussion).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a critique of the Paquin and Adams study.

claims.claim: Adaptive diversification is common in experimental evolution due to spatial structuring and metabolic diversification.
claims.source: Indeed, adaptive diversification is common in experimental evolution due to spatial structuring (Rainey and Travisano, 1998; Frenkel et al., 2015) and metabolic diversification (Paquin and Adams, 1983; Helling et al., 1987; Turner et al., 1996; Spencer et al., 2008; Kinnersley et al., 2014), and is typically maintained by negative frequency-dependent selection, in which rare genotypes are favored.
claims.evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to experimental evolution studies.

claims.claim: Positive frequency-dependent selection is not typically observed in experimental evolution.
claims.source: Positive frequency-dependent selection, in contrast, is not typically observed in experimental evolution.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a general observation about experimental evolution.

claims.claim: Negative frequency-dependent selection is more commonly observed in experimental evolution than positive frequency-dependent selection.
claims.source: Of the two, negative frequency-dependent selection is more commonly observed in experimental evolution, arising, for example, from nutrient cross-feeding (Helling et al., 1987; Turner et al., 1996; Spencer et al., 2008; Kinnersley et al., 2014; Plucain et al., 2014; Green et al., 2020) and spatial structuring (Rainey and Travisano, 1998; Frenkel et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: A crowded, structured environment provides an opportunity for allelopathies to offer a local advantage.
claims.source: A crowded, structured environment provides an opportunity for allelopathies to offer a local advantage.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a general principle.

claims.claim: Killer toxin has been shown to impart frequency-dependent selection in structured environments due to a high local concentration of secreted toxin.
claims.source: Killer toxin has been shown to impart frequency-dependent selection in structured environments due to a high local concentration of secreted toxin (Greig and Travisano, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citation to Greig and Travisano, 2008.

claims.claim: Nontransitivity in the experimental system is due, in part, to interference competition.
claims.source: Nontransitivity in our experimental system is due, in part, to interference competition.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: Interference competition can drive ecological nontransitivity.
claims.source: Interference competition can drive ecological nontransitivity (Kerr et al., 2002; Kirkup and Riley, 2004), suggesting that similar mechanisms may underlie both ecological and genealogical nontransitivity.
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to Kerr et al., 2002 and Kirkup and Riley, 2004.

claims.claim: The adaptive evolution of genealogical nontransitivity does not follow the canonical model of a co-evolutionary arms race.
claims.source: The adaptive evolution of genealogical nontransitivity in our system does not follow the canonical model of a co-evolutionary arms race where the host evolves mechanisms to prevent the selfish replication of the virus and the virus evolves to circumvent the host's defenses (Daugherty and Malik, 2012; Rowley, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to Daugherty and Malik, 2012 and Rowley, 2017.

claims.claim: Mutations that fix in the viral and yeast populations do so because they provide a direct fitness advantage in their respective populations.
claims.source: Rather, mutations that fix in the viral and yeast populations do so because they provide a direct fitness advantage in their respective populations.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the results.

claims.claim: Nearly all mutations in toxin-resistance genes are nonsynonymous (18 nonsense/frameshift, 21 missense, one synonymous).
claims.source: Nearly all mutations in these toxin-resistance genes are nonsynonymous (18 nonsense/frameshift, 21 missense, one synonymous), indicating a strong signature of positive selection.
claims.evidence: This is stated with mutation counts indicating positive selection.

claims.claim: The nuclear genome adapts in response to the presence of the killer toxin.
claims.source: This suggests that the nuclear genome adapts in response to the presence of the killer toxin; however, the effect of these mutations may be beyond the resolution of our fitness assay.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment of mutations in toxin-resistance genes.

claims.claim: Defective interfering particles are thought to outcompete full-length virus due to their decreased replication time.
claims.source: These defective interfering particles are thought to outcompete full-length virus due to their decreased replication time (Kane et al., 1979; Ridley and Wickner, 1983; Esteban and Wickner, 1988).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to Kane et al., 1979, Ridley and Wickner, 1983, and Esteban and Wickner, 1988.

claims.claim: Defective interfering particles are common to RNA viruses.
claims.source: Defective interfering particles are common to RNA viruses (Holland et al., 1982).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citation to Holland et al., 1982.

claims.claim: There are several different killer viruses in yeast (e.g. K1, K2, K28, and Klus), each of which arose independently and has a distinct mechanism of action.
claims.source: Though there are several different killer viruses in yeast (e.g. K1, K2, K28, and Klus), each arose independently and has a distinct mechanism of action (Rodríguez-Cousiño et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citation to Rodríguez-Cousiño et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Nontransitive interactions may arise frequently through cycles of gains and losses of toxin production and toxin immunity in lineages that contain RNA viruses.
claims.source: Nontransitive interactions may therefore arise frequently through cycles of gains and losses of toxin production and toxin immunity in lineages that contain RNA viruses.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the findings.

claims.claim: Reports of nontransitivity arising along evolutionary lines of descent are rare.
claims.source: Reports of nontransitivity arising along evolutionary lines of descent are rare (de Visser and Lenski, 2002; Beaumont et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to de Visser and Lenski, 2002 and Beaumont et al., 2009.

claims.claim: The Paquin and Adams experiment was correctly interpreted under the assumption that large asexual populations evolved by clonal replacement.
claims.source: This experiment was correctly interpreted under the assumption—generally accepted at the time—that large asexual populations evolved by clonal replacement, where new beneficial mutations arise and quickly sweep to fixation.
claims.evidence: This is stated as historical context for the Paquin and Adams study.

claims.claim: The strong selection/weak mutation model is now known to be an oversimplification for large asexual populations.
claims.source: This strong selection/weak mutation model, however, is now known to be an oversimplification for large asexual populations, where multiple beneficial mutations arise and spread simultaneously through the population leading to extensive clonal interference (Gerrish and Lenski, 1998; Kvitek and Sherlock, 2013; Lang et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to Gerrish and Lenski, 1998, Kvitek and Sherlock, 2013, and Lang et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The duration of the Paquin and Adams experiment was too short for the number of reported selective sweeps to have occurred.
claims.source: In addition, the duration of the Paquin and Adams experiment was too short for the number of reported selective sweeps to have occurred (4 in 245 generations and 6 in 305 generations, for haploids and diploids, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a critique of the Paquin and Adams study.

claims.claim: The strongest known beneficial mutations in glucose-limited chemostats, hexose transporter amplifications, provide a fitness advantage of ~30%.
claims.source: The strongest known beneficial mutations in glucose-limited chemostats, hexose transporter amplifications, provide a fitness advantage of ~30% (Gresham et al., 2008; Kvitek and Sherlock, 2011) and would require a minimum of ~150 generations to fix in a population size of 4 × 109 (Otto and Whitlock, 1997).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to Gresham et al., 2008, Kvitek and Sherlock, 2011, and Otto and Whitlock, 1997.

claims.claim: Paquin and Adams observed nontransitive interactions among contemporaneous lineages—ecological nontransitivity—rather than nontransitivity among genealogical descendants.
claims.source: We contend that Paquin and Adams observed nontransitive interactions among contemporaneous lineages—ecological nontransitivity—rather than nontransitivity among genealogical descendants.
claims.evidence: This is stated as the authors' interpretation of the Paquin and Adams study.

claims.claim: Apart from the present study, there are no other examples of nontransitivity arising along a line descent.
claims.source: Apart from the present study, there are no other examples of nontransitivity arising along a line descent, but numerous examples of nontransitive interactions among contemporaneous lineages (Sinervo and Lively, 1996; Kerr et al., 2002; Kirkup and Riley, 2004; Károlyi et al., 2005; Laird and Schamp, 2006; Reichenbach et al., 2007; Precoda et al., 2017; Menezes et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to studies of ecological nontransitivity.

claims.claim: The continuous action of selection can give rise to genotypes that are less fit compared to a distant ancestor.
claims.source: Our results show that the continuous action of selection can give rise to genotypes that are less fit compared to a distant ancestor.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claims.claim: Nontransitive interactions can arise quickly due to multilevel selection in a host/virus system.
claims.source: We show that nontransitive interactions can arise quickly due to multilevel selection in a host/virus system.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claims.claim: Multi-level selection is common in the context of this experiment—most yeast populations fix nuclear and viral variants by Generation 1000.
claims.source: In the context of this experiment multi-level selection is common—most yeast populations fix nuclear and viral variants by Generation 1000.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claims.claim: Adaptive evolution is capable of giving rise to nontransitive fitness interactions along an evolutionary lineage, even under simple laboratory conditions.
claims.source: Overall, our results demonstrate that adaptive evolution is capable of giving rise to nontransitive fitness interactions along an evolutionary lineage, even under simple laboratory conditions.
claims.evidence: This is stated as the main conclusion of the study.

results.result: Nontransitive fitness interactions arose in population BYS1-D08 over 1000 generations. The Intermediate clone (Gen 335) is 3.8% fitter than the Early clone (Gen 0), and the Late clone (Gen 1000) is 1.2% fitter than the Intermediate clone, yet the Late clone exhibits frequency-dependent fitness disadvantage against the Early clone. This nontransitivity results from beneficial nuclear mutations (yur1, ste4) combined with stepwise viral deterioration.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C7, C11-C12, C14, C46-C47 provide converging evidence for nontransitivity through fitness measurements at multiple starting frequencies (Figure 1B), virus-curing experiments demonstrating the role of the killer virus, and consistency with previously measured effects of nuclear mutations. The mechanistic explanation linking nuclear adaptation and viral deterioration is well-supported by experimental manipulations.

results.result: The killer phenotype changed stepwise during evolution of BYS1-D08: the ancestral Early clone exhibits killing ability and immunity (K+I+), the Intermediate clone lost killing ability but retained immunity (K-I+), and the Late clone lost both killing ability and immunity (K-I-). Viral mutations are sufficient to explain these phenotypic changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C10 document the phenotypic progression using halo assays (Figures 1A, 1—figure supplement 2-3), and C38 demonstrates sufficiency through cytoduction experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) where transferred viral variants confer the expected phenotypes. The experimental design appropriately isolates viral from nuclear contributions.

results.result: Approximately half of 142 evolved yeast populations lost or weakened killing ability by Generation 1000, with ~10% losing both killing and immunity. Loss of immunity without loss of killing was never observed. This indicates that multilevel selection (fixing both nuclear and viral mutations) is common under these experimental conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C17 are directly supported by phenotypic screening data (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) across 142 populations. Claims C3 and C87 extend this to conclude multilevel selection is common, which is well-supported by the high frequency of phenotypic changes attributable to viral evolution combined with known nuclear adaptation.

results.result: Viral genome sequencing revealed that populations losing killing ability possess 1-3 mutations in the M1 killer virus coding sequence (mostly missense), while control populations retaining the killer phenotype had only one synonymous mutation. There is strong statistical correlation (p=1.4×10⁻¹³) between viral mutations and loss of killing ability, with an estimated half of all populations fixing phenotype-altering viral variants by Generation 1000.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C26 are supported by viral genome sequencing data from 67 populations (Figure 3A). The strong statistical correlation (C25) and stark contrast between experimental and control populations (C23-C24) provide compelling evidence. The estimate in C26 is reasonable given the data, though it relies on extrapolation from the sequenced subset.

results.result: Among populations that lost killing ability, 42 of 57 fixed one of three single nucleotide polymorphisms (D106G, D253N, I292M), which likely existed at low frequency in the ancestral culture. An additional 34 putative de novo point mutations arose during evolution of individual populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C29 are supported by sequencing data (Supplementary file 1) and detection of D106G in early clones (C28). The inference that common polymorphisms were ancestral standing variation is reasonable given their high frequency and detection in founding populations. The distinction between standing variation and de novo mutations is appropriately made.

results.result: The K1 coding sequence shows balancing selection (dN/dS = 0.90) and extreme transition:transversion bias (R = 6.4, p<0.0001). This bias appears specific to viral genomes, as nuclear genomes show much lower ratios (R = 0.8), suggesting a mutational bias of the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C32 are supported by mutational spectrum analysis (Supplementary file 2) with appropriate statistical tests. The comparison to nuclear genome mutation patterns (C32) and citation of similar patterns in other viral systems strengthens the interpretation. The dN/dS ratio and transition bias are clearly documented.

results.result: Two viral genomes with large deletions in the K1 ORF were detected. These deletion mutants maintain cis signals for replication and packaging, and coexist with full-length viral variants in the same populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C35 are supported by sequencing data (Figure 3B) and appropriate citations for the functional requirements of deletion mutants (C34). The observation of coexistence (C35) is important for understanding within-host viral dynamics and is clearly stated.

results.result: Viral sweeps often coincide with nuclear sweeps in time-course data. Since nuclear sweeps contain known driver mutations, viral variants may be hitchhiking rather than driving adaptation. Consistent with this, the Intermediate clone's viral variant confers no significant fitness effect compared to the ancestral virus.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C37 are supported by time-course sequencing (Figure 4) showing temporal coincidence of sweeps. Claim C13 provides experimental support through virus-swapping experiments (Figure 1B). The hitchhiking hypothesis is appropriately presented as a possibility (C37) rather than certainty, and is well-supported by the lack of fitness effect in C13.

results.result: Frequency-dependent selection was observed when one competitor had killing ability and the other lacked immunity. However, when killer phenotypes were compatible, host fitness was unaffected by viral variant identity or even virus presence, suggesting no detectable fitness cost of toxin production or virus maintenance.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41 are supported by systematic competition experiments with cytoductants (Figure 5A). The experimental design appropriately tests different phenotypic combinations. The inference of no fitness cost (C41) is reasonable given the data, though the resolution of the fitness assay should be considered when interpreting negative results.

results.result: In intracellular competition experiments using heteroplasmic diploids, evolved viral variants outcompeted ancestral variants, with derived variants fixing in most lines. A de novo G131D variant arose and swept in one line. This demonstrates that viral variants have selective advantage within individual cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C45 are supported by intracellular competition experiments with appropriate controls to minimize among-cell selection (Figure 5B-C). The use of both Sanger and Illumina sequencing (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) strengthens confidence in frequency estimates. The observation of de novo variants arising during the experiment (C44) provides additional evidence for ongoing intracellular selection.

results.result: Nuclear genomes show statistical enrichment of mutations in β-glucan biosynthesis genes (6-fold, p<0.0001) and genes conferring K1 toxin resistance (40 mutations in 11 of 36 genes, p=1.8×10⁻⁵). Nearly all mutations in toxin-resistance genes are nonsynonymous (18 nonsense/frameshift, 21 missense, 1 synonymous). However, these mutations are not sufficient to account for loss of killing ability or immunity.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C20, C72-C73 are supported by appropriate statistical tests and mutation counts. The enrichment analyses are properly conducted with significant p-values. Claim C20 appropriately notes that despite enrichment, these nuclear mutations don't explain the phenotypic changes, which is consistent with the viral mutation data. The signature of positive selection (C72) is clear.

results.result: Nontransitivity in this system arises through interference competition rather than a co-evolutionary arms race. Mutations fix in viral and yeast populations because they provide direct fitness advantages in their respective populations, not through antagonistic host-virus coevolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 provide a mechanistic interpretation supported by the experimental data. The distinction from canonical arms race dynamics (C70) is appropriate given that viral deterioration (not increased virulence) is observed. The interpretation that mutations provide direct fitness benefits (C71) is supported by the intracellular competition data and lack of fitness costs.

results.result: The continuous action of selection can give rise to genotypes less fit than distant ancestors. Nontransitive interactions can arise quickly through multilevel selection in host/virus systems. Adaptive evolution is capable of producing nontransitive fitness interactions along evolutionary lineages, even under simple laboratory conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C86, C88 represent the main conclusions of the study and are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence including fitness measurements, phenotypic tracking, genome sequencing, and mechanistic experiments. The demonstration spans multiple levels (nuclear and viral) and multiple populations, providing robust support for these broad conclusions.

results.result: The authors reinterpret the Paquin and Adams (1983) study, arguing that it likely observed ecological nontransitivity among contemporaneous lineages rather than genealogical nontransitivity. This reinterpretation is based on modern understanding of clonal interference and the implausibly short time for the reported number of selective sweeps.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62, C79-C83 provide a critical reanalysis of prior work. The critique is well-reasoned, citing modern understanding of population genetics (C80) and providing quantitative arguments about sweep dynamics (C81-C82). The reinterpretation (C83) is appropriately presented as the authors' contention rather than definitive proof, and is supported by sound reasoning.

results.result: Methodological details of the evolution experiment and fitness assays are provided, including daily 1:210 dilutions (10 generations/day, effective population size ~10⁵), clone isolation at generations coinciding with selective sweep completion, and 50-generation competition assays with fitness calculated from log-ratio slopes.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C94 describe methodological details that are clearly stated in the Materials and methods section with appropriate citations to previous work (Lang et al., 2011, 2013). These methods are standard for experimental evolution studies and are described with sufficient detail for reproducibility.
